sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

content.text:
Case N44: segment the peripheral nerve sheath tumor on this T2-weighted MRI.

Volume: 141x141x82 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

case N44 | sequence T2 | shape (i,j,k)=(141, 141, 82) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: peripheral nerve sheath tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).
axial 41/82 | crop full | marks none | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 1/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking: The axial slice shows a well-circumscribed ovoid mass with a capsule, which looks like the likely PNST. I want to verify this by checking the axial slice with marks first before confirming.

content.text: sheet axial 5–78/82 (12 slices) | v0 | tool calls 2/40, prompts 0/15
sheet coronal 20–120/141 (12 slices) | v0 | tool calls 3/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm wondering if the round structure at this axial level could actually be the humeral head with its glenoid articulation, given the bright rim and intermediate signal pattern, though I'm second-guessing whether that matches typical marrow signal on fat-suppressed T2.

Tracking the shaft narrowing from slice 58-78 and the head widening around 18-38 helps confirm this is normal humeral anatomy rather than a lesion, with the bright crescent likely representing joint fluid near the glenoid. I'm trying to orient left/right to figure out whether this is a right or left shoulder based on medial glenoid positioning.

Though actually I should reconsider the anatomy entirely — the coronal images show a rounded structure with skin wrapping inferiorly and striated muscle resembling deltoid coverage, which could suggest a shoulder, but the orientation seems unusual enough that I'm wondering if this could instead be a knee, heel, or another joint like the calcaneus based on how the fat and bone appear in the sagittal view.

Tracing the ball-to-shaft pattern upward in coronal makes me wonder if this is flipped from a typical shoulder orientation, or possibly a hip with the femoral head and neck instead. But I'm also reconsidering whether this is bone at all — it could be a peripheral nerve sheath tumor, a round encapsulated mass with a dark rim mimicking cortex and a split fat sign, rather than true osseous anatomy.

Scanning the axial series, I'm checking for small bright spots adjacent to the ball on T2 that could represent the actual lesion rather than the bone itself — the ball appears intermediate-to-dark and homogeneous like marrow, with a dark cortical rim and a bright crescent likely representing joint fluid, so I'm now looking elsewhere, at these peripheral bright foci across slices 38-58, for the true tumor.

That bright spot could be a vessel like the posterior circumflex humeral artery or possibly the axillary nerve itself in the quadrilateral space, which would fit a small schwannoma. I'm also reconsidering whether this is actually the knee rather than the shoulder, since the coronal slices show a large rounded striated structure that could be gastrocnemius muscle, though deltoid wrapping around the humeral head remains equally plausible if the image orientation is flipped.

Scanning further coronal slices, I notice a round structure with a bright crescent and heterogeneous interior, and another small oval structure with a dark rim and bright spot that might correspond to what I saw on axial images — I should check the sagittal series next to clarify this finding.

content.text: sheet sagittal 20–125/141 (12 slices) | v0 | tool calls 4/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm noticing inconsistent findings across slices—different sized oval structures with dark rims appearing in sagittal 49, 58, and 96—which makes the anatomy hard to pin down. The image is a small 141x141x82 crop at 1mm resolution, so I'm trying to figure out what region this actually represents.

The crop is likely centered on a lesion, with the big ovoid structure near volume center (70,70,41) across axial, coronal, and sagittal views being the prime candidate. I'm now second-guessing whether this represents a soft tissue mass with a thin capsule versus a bone shaft like humerus or femur, since the ring diameter measurements (~17mm) don't quite match typical shaft sizes, and I'm also considering whether this could instead be near the glenoid based on other axial slices.

I'm reconsidering the anatomy — the bright crescent beside the ball structure plus dark diagonal lines suggest the scapular body/neck extending posteromedially from the glenoid, making the ball the humeral head, which would make this a left shoulder given the orientation. That means increasing axial slice index likely corresponds to moving inferiorly from the humeral head toward the shaft.

But then I notice the coronal display is labeled "superior TOP," which seems to conflict with the ball appearing near the bottom with structures extending upward — unless the slice indexing runs the opposite direction, meaning higher axial numbers are actually superior rather than inferior. That raises the question of whether I'm even looking at a shoulder at all, or possibly a different joint like the elbow or knee instead.

Reconsidering the anatomy, the "ball" might just be the lesion itself rather than a true anatomic joint surface — a fusiform peripheral nerve sheath tumor tapering where the nerve enters and exits would look exactly like this, and the thickened dark rim I'm seeing around 17mm could represent the nerve segment feeding into it. I want to re-examine the coronal images more carefully, since there seems to be a separate rounded structure to the left that could be the glenoid, distinct from the ball-shaped lesion. I should pull up a single larger, higher-resolution view of one slice to resolve this ambiguity.

content.text: coronal 75/141 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 5/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
Checking the scale of the coronal view, I'm examining slice 75 where there's a large oval structure in the middle with a dark rim and a bright crescent along its left edge.

Looking at the lower axial slices, the structure tapers from the larger ball into a smaller ring with a thick dark wall by slices 58-78, suggesting a tubular shape rather than an isolated mass. This tapering pattern — ball narrowing into a shaft-like structure — makes me reconsider whether this could be bone (humeral head to neck to shaft) rather than a pure soft-tissue schwannoma, especially since the ball's signal is darker than the fat and closer to muscle, which is somewhat atypical for a typical T2-hyperintense PNST.

Measuring the ball's actual span in axial 32, I get around 54mm, which fits better with a femoral or humeral head size than a smaller joint structure. The bright crescent I'm seeing could be joint fluid between the head and socket, and I'm cross-checking the coronal image for cortical lines that might clarify which joint this is.

The fine radiating dark lines near the top of several axial slices look like deltoid muscle striations or intramuscular tendon septa, with a lens-shaped muscle bounded by fascia and a bright subcutaneous fat layer outside it — suggesting this ball is the humeral head wrapped by the deltoid anteriorly and laterally, which points toward a shoulder joint rather than a hip.

Now I'm hunting for the actual lesion — a small bright oval near the lateral surgical neck of the humerus under the deltoid could sit right where the axillary nerve wraps around posteriorly, making a schwannoma there plausible, and there's also a bright ring posterolaterally that might just be the circumflex vessels rather than nerve pathology.

I try mapping the bright spot's pixel coordinates back to voxel space to see if it aligns with a lesion-centered crop, but the numbers don't quite line up with a centered crop. So I reconsider whether the large ball itself is simply humeral head marrow rather than the lesion — comparing its intensity to the humeral shaft marrow on another slice, they look similar, which argues against the ball being pathological. I move to checking the coronal view to see what surrounds the ball's lateral and inferior surfaces.

Looking at the structures near the ball at the bottom of coronal 75, I try to figure out if the dark and bright bands there correspond to acromion, deltoid, fat, and skin layers, but the anatomy isn't resolving cleanly from these marks. I decide to pull up axial 51 again with full annotation to get a clearer look at that bright spot.

content.text: axial 52/82 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 6/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
At axial slice 52, I'm identifying the humeral head/neck by its rounded cortex, then tracing a diagonal dark band running from upper-right to lower-left that could be the subscapularis muscle or possibly the coracoid/clavicle region.

Actually, reconsidering this entirely — the striated top region suggests a pectoralis/deltoid muscle, which makes me question whether I'm even looking at a shoulder. The round structure with a bright adjacent oval (possibly a bursa, vessel, or small schwannoma) and posterior bright vessels makes me wonder if this is actually a hip: the femoral head with acetabulum medially, iliopsoas/sartorius anteriorly, and gluteus maximus posteriorly as the large mottled muscle mass. I'm also weighing whether the "thick dark rim" is instead the lower pole of a tumor rather than normal anatomy.

I'm checking the cortex thickness across slices to decide — at axial 52 the rim is thick, while at axial 78 it's thinner and ring-shaped, consistent with bone cortex rather than tumor capsule. I'm now trying to trace the bright oval's extent across axial, sagittal, and coronal views to determine whether it's a small isolated structure spanning roughly 8-10mm, and plan to check the coronal slice through that same marker next.

So the shaft-like structure sits superior to the ball, which seems odd for a humerus unless the arm is abducted overhead — maybe I'm looking at a different bone entirely. I need to re-examine coronal 75, where the ball sits at bottom center with a darker "neck" region rising above it between two dark landmarks.

Looking more closely, above the ball there's a gray zone rising to the top, with a separate rounded structure to the left that resembles muscle. The bright band hugging the ball on the right and bottom looks like fat, which would place the ball very close to skin laterally with only a thin fat layer — but for a true humeral head, deltoid muscle should be between the head and skin laterally, which doesn't quite match what I'm seeing in axial 52.

I'm now reconsidering whether this could instead be the thigh or buttock, with the ball representing a tumor rather than a joint. Reviewing axial 41, coronal 70, and sagittal 70 overviews, I note the bright crescent and vessel clumps near the ball, the anterior muscle abutting it with a fascial plane between them, its dark rim with surrounding fat, and the posterior dark region on sagittal view — all details I need to weigh before settling on an anatomic interpretation.

I'm also checking the inferior axial slices (5-12) for bony contours, like a possible heel structure near the center and a dark ovoid ring near the bottom — this could be a bone ring. I think I need to pull up the full sagittal 70 series with markers to trace continuity between the ball and the shaft-like structure before drawing conclusions.

content.text: sagittal 72/141 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 7/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
In sagittal slice 72, I'm tracing the ball's position in the lower-center region, bounded by a dark posterior line and another dark anterior line that seems to connect the ball to a structure extending upward.

This makes me wonder if the volume is oriented with superior-inferior flipped—like the humeral head capped by deltoid muscle appearing inferior rather than superior. If so, the dark curvilinear structures and ovoid ring I'm seeing at axial slice 12 could actually be the acromion, clavicle, and AC joint, which would make sense anatomically if the orientation is reversed.

So the normal anatomy would be: top-of-shoulder structures near axial 5, humeral head around 18-38, glenoid neck around 45-52, and surgical neck/shaft from 58-78, with the scapula running diagonally posteromedial at the glenoid level. That makes the ball a normal humeral head, which means the lesion in question is something separate—possibly an axillary nerve schwannoma given its position lateral to the surgical neck, deep to the deltoid, which matches where that nerve wraps around the humerus. I'm now checking whether the lesion's position is roughly centered in the crop, calculating its offset from the volume center in all three axes to see how far off-center it actually sits.

I'm now tracking this bright oval across multiple axial slices (45, 52, 58) and it seems to consistently appear at the lateral aspect of the humeral head/neck, which supports it being a real, persistent structure rather than noise. I'm also cross-checking a sagittal image to see if there's a corresponding elongated bright spot near the superior end that would corroborate its location in 3D.

But when I try to convert the sagittal slice index into x-coordinates, I realize the sagittal index I'm looking at doesn't actually line up with the x-position of the finding I identified in the axial views, so I need to recheck my pixel-to-voxel scaling math on the axial display before trusting this cross-reference.

Sagittal sheet 58 showed something like an oval roughly 8mm posterior to the ball, though I'm not confident in that reading. Let me check the sagittal slice around i≈90 instead — sheet 87 showed the ball with a bright crescent posterior-inferior, but the oval wasn't clearly visible there, so I should look at sagittal 90 with the marks to confirm.

content.text: sagittal 90/141 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 8/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
Looking at the sagittal 90 image, I'm trying to identify the structures around the ball — the bright crescent of joint fluid posteriorly and whether the darker structure behind it is the glenoid, comparing this to what the glenoid would look like on axial slices.

I'm reconsidering whether the ball is actually a schwannoma rather than bone marrow — schwannomas on T2 are usually heterogeneously bright, while this ball looks homogeneous and intermediate in intensity, closer to muscle than fat, which argues against it being yellow marrow unless this is a child with red marrow or there's uneven fat suppression. I'm also checking whether the bright peripheral band in the images is subcutaneous fat by looking at the signal intensities at the outer edges near the skin surface.

I notice the posterior region shows mottled brightness, which I suspect is coil-proximity bias rather than true tissue signal, since the patient is lying on the coil and posterior structures pick up more signal — meaning the intensities across the image aren't uniform and need correction for position. I'm now looking at the dark rim around the ball, considering whether its thickness is consistent with humeral cortex plus chemical shift artifact, and tracing the diagonal dark lines near the ball to see if they correspond to the scapular neck with a bright crescent between them.

This whole pattern — round humeral head, crescent fluid, thin dark glenoid lines running posteromedially, scapular body as a faint line — matches a classic axial shoulder view, with the two diverging dark lines likely representing subscapularis and infraspinatus around the scapula. Since the joint itself looks normal, I'm now searching elsewhere in the volume for the actual lesion, considering bright spots at various axial and sagittal slices as candidates, and wondering if this crop comes from a whole-body MRI dataset of NF1 patients where tumors can appear in varying sizes and locations.

Checking the center of the cropped volume, I notice it lands almost exactly on the humeral head, which would be odd unless the crop was centered on something there — raising the possibility that the "ball" I'm seeing is actually the lesion itself, perhaps a large schwannoma in the axilla or brachial plexus region mimicking the joint, abutting the scapula.

But then I need to find the actual humerus separately. Looking at the thick-rimmed ring structure in axial 52, its diameter (~32mm) is plausible for a humeral surgical neck, so I'm trying to trace whether this ring connects continuously to the ball in the coronal views.

In coronal 84 there's a ball at bottom with a vertical dark line above it, and coronal 93 shows a smaller oval near the bottom-right — but if axial index increases superiorly, the ball sits inferior to the shaft, which wouldn't make sense anatomically for a normal standing humerus if the ball is meant to be the humeral head.

I'm trying other possibilities: femoral head with the neck, acetabular roof, patella, calcaneus, talar dome — none quite fit the ring-above-ball pattern I'm seeing. I keep coming back to the shoulder, maybe with the arm in an unusual position, but I'm not settled yet.

Reconsidering the imaging sequence — if this is a STIR/fat-sat MRI for NF1-related nerve sheath tumors, the bright nodules I'm spotting near the humeral neck posteriorly could represent small plexiform neurofibromas tracking along the axillary nerve through the quadrilateral space, rather than one single structure.

But the task calls for segmenting a single peripheral nerve sheath tumor, so I'm trying to pin down whether the "ball" and the "ring" I keep spotting in different slices are actually the same continuous structure. I'm cross-checking the vertical position of the ring's center in axial 52 against the ball's center in axial 41 to see if their coordinates line up across slices.

Looking at coronal 75, I'm trying to trace whether the tissue above the ball connects into that ring-like tube, but the dark cortical borders aren't convincing me it's a clean continuous tube — I'm only seeing a partial dark edge on the left and bright subcutaneous tissue on the right, nothing conclusive. With plenty of calls left in budget, I'll check axial 65 next to get a clearer look at how the ring structure relates to its surroundings.

content.text: axial 66/82 | crop full | marks none | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 9/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm looking at axial slice 66, identifying the humeral shaft by its thick dark cortex, with surrounding muscles medially and what appear to be axillary vessels or brachial plexus elements as bright tubular structures nearby.

The posterior region shows mottled brightness consistent with triceps and posterior muscles, while a dark curved area at the bottom-left suggests chest wall or thorax, placing the axilla there. This raises a puzzle: if the humeral shaft sits at axial 52-78 and a rounded structure appears at axial 18-38, the orientation seems inconsistent for it to simply be the humeral head continuous with the shaft—unless I'm misreading superior/inferior direction, or that ball is actually something else entirely, like a mass rather than normal anatomy. I want to check axial 45 to see how that dark-cortex ball connects through the intervening slices.

Tracking through the slices, I see a thick posterior-left rim and a connection to a scapula-like band, with the ball persisting as a single coaxial structure with the shaft rather than sitting beside it—this confirms it's the humeral head, and the image must be flipped so that increasing axial index corresponds to inferior direction, regardless of what the header claims. This fits with the chest wall/axilla appearing medially at lower slices and the acromion appearing superiorly near axial 5-12, so the ball is just normal bone and the tumor I'm looking for must be located somewhere else in the volume.

Now I'm scanning for a plexiform neurofibroma along the brachial plexus or axillary nerve, looking at bright tubular and lobulated structures near the axilla across several slices that could be either tumor tissue or just slow-flowing veins lighting up on T2 fat-sat. I keep coming back to a small, very bright ~8mm round focus near the anterolateral humeral neck under the deltoid, trying to decide whether it represents something like subdeltoid bursa fluid near the bicipital groove or an actual lesion.

There are too many normal structures mimicking pathology, so I'm widening my search through the coronal series toward both the anterior and posterior extremes, looking for something more clearly abnormal than these vascular and tendon-sheath confounders.

I'm also re-checking the sagittal slices near the ball's center and medial side — small dark ovals paired with bright spots that could represent the coracoid process or another bony landmark rather than true pathology, tracing their position relative to the joint to figure out what anatomic structure they actually correspond to.

Could be the coracoid instead. I'm wondering about the actual dataset here — likely a peripheral nerve sheath tumor dataset with 141x141x82 crops at 1mm isotropic, where the lesion itself might be large and centered near the humeral head rather than the ball being purely anatomical.

Looking closer at axial slice 45, I notice a thick dark rim along the posterior side of the ball merging into an irregular dark mass toward the glenoid/scapular neck area, plus a bright ring nearby. I'm questioning whether this dark irregular structure represents a tumor mass rather than normal joint anatomy, and whether a true joint space is even visible here.

The bright crescent spanning roughly a third of the ball's circumference on the posteromedial side, followed by a thin dark line and triangular scapular neck shape, suggests I'm looking at the humeral head articulating with the glenoid. In axial 32, two dark lines diverge toward the left edge forming a triangle — possibly the anterior and posterior cortices of the scapula, though a scapula should present as a single plate rather than two separate lines.

Actually, these diverging lines might instead be fascial planes of the subscapularis muscle rather than bony cortex, since the gray region between them looks intermediate in intensity like soft tissue. I'll need to pull up axial 32 at full resolution to sort this out properly.

content.text: axial 33/82 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 10/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
Looking at axial slice 33, I'm examining the ball's anatomy — a thin dark rim, a bright crescent on the posteromedial side, and a triangular fat/gray region near where two dark lines converge inferiorly. The anterior muscle shows intramuscular septa, likely deltoid, with a large posterior muscle mass behind it, though the ball itself seems larger than expected for a humeral head.

I'm trying to figure out whether the medial triangular region represents the glenoid — typically it would show a pear-shaped bone with marrow and a labrum, but here I don't see a clear bony structure, just a mottled gray triangle bounded by thin dark lines, with the bright crescent sitting between the head and a faint dark line that might be glenoid cartilage or cortex. Below the horizontal dark line, the posterior region appears bright and mottled, possibly reflecting coil bias in the image.

Looking posteriorly I notice a dark oval structure that could be a vessel flow void surrounded by bright signal, plus a dark vertical line running down from the ball that looks like fascia.
